solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Post spy outside English royal house

parts.note: to post someone somewhere is to plant them there

explanation.surface: An espionage plot: a spy is stationed just outside the palace of an English royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: "Post spy" reads as one order to station a spy, but each word is its own piece, and "English" is the letter hidden inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plantagenets were the royal house that ruled England from Henry II to Richard III.

clue.text: Time to abandon bet? That's a joke

parts.note: a punt is a bet (British slang)

explanation.surface: Someone told it is time to give up gambling replies that the idea is laughable.
explanation.walkthrough: A punt is British slang for a wager; drop its T and the joke is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun is a joke built on a word's double sense or sound.

clue.text: Trouble in the past overwhelming centre of Zagreb

indicators.note: take the middle letters of Zagreb

parts.note: the two middle letters of ZaGReb

explanation.surface: A historical note about unrest that once engulfed the Croatian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Zagreb has six letters, so its centre is a pair, GR, not a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for aggressive trouble or hassle.

clue.text: Birds ultimately flaunt it over rodents

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first pieces sit over the rodents
take the last letter of flaunt

explanation.surface: Birds finally show off in front of the mice below them.
explanation.walkthrough: "it" is taken literally, and the birds show off by sitting over the mice in the column.
explanation.definitionFit: Titmice, or tits, are small songbirds.

clue.text: Good to get involved again: it should bear fruit

parts.note: to re-engage is to get involved again

explanation.surface: A pep talk: getting back into things is good and will pay off.
explanation.walkthrough: "Bear fruit" pretends to mean succeed, echoing the pep-talk surface, but a greengage tree literally bears fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A greengage is a plum tree, which bears the green plums of the same name.

clue.text: Scandinavian goddesses, and not Poles

parts.note: the North and South poles, N and S

explanation.surface: A clarification that these northern goddesses are not from Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: "Poles" wants to be the people of Poland; here it is the two magnetic poles, N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norns are the three goddesses of fate in Norse mythology.

clue.text: Support premier accepting Republican crown

parts.note: a golf tee supports the ball

explanation.surface: Politics: backing a prime minister who has taken the Republican crown.
explanation.walkthrough: "Crown" is set up as a political prize, but it is the crown of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanists call the leafy upper part of a tree its crown, the part a royal crown sits on for a person.

clue.text: Nip backwards and forwards serving fizzy drink

indicators.note: the word reads the same either way

parts.note: to nip is to make a quick trip, into a shop or out for a moment

explanation.surface: A barman darting to and fro handing out fizzy drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: To nip into a shop is to pop into it, and POP reads the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Named for the sound the cork or cap makes, pop is the informal word for a carbonated soft drink.

clue.text: So a plant's unexpectedly situated behind a hooter

indicators.note: the letters turn up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Someone surprised to find a plant placed behind a car horn.
explanation.walkthrough: A hooter is British slang for a nose, not the car horn the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Postnasal means situated behind the nose, as in postnasal drip.

clue.text: Spreader of alarm, one who sells grass?

explanation.surface: An alarmist is likened to someone dealing cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: Panic is a genus of grass (panic grass), so a seller of it would be a panic-monger; the question mark flags the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: A panicmonger stirs up alarm, spreading panic.

clue.text: Tailored thing you and I regularly assume at first when retiring

definitions.text: Tailored thing you and I regularly assume at first when retiring

indicators.note: take the first letters of regularly and assume
those two letters go backwards
THING is cut and restyled into new order

explanation.surface: A description of pyjamas: the fitted garment we routinely put on when going to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: nightwear is what you and I regularly put on when retiring to bed. "Retiring" does double duty as bedtime and reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightwear is clothing worn in bed, which is exactly what we assume on retiring.

clue.text: Headland backing on east German city

indicators.note: the headland word reads backwards

parts.note: a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's shores or Orford Ness

explanation.surface: A coastal promontory lying behind the east side of a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: Ness is an old word for a headland, common in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is a large city in Germany's Ruhr.

clue.text: Ideal article on posh tropical headgear

indicators.note: in an across clue, the article comes after the posh headgear

parts.note: a topi is a sun helmet

explanation.surface: A remark that a fancy tropical hat is the perfect accessory.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a crossword staple; a topi is the pith helmet of the colonial tropics.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopian means ideal, like the perfect society of More's Utopia.

clue.text: Subscriber runs in without a plan?

explanation.surface: A magazine subscriber who signs up on impulse.
explanation.walkthrough: "Subscriber" means one who signs underneath, not one who buys a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: The undersigned is the person who has signed, literally subscribed, the document.

clue.text: Diabolical cast in a play

indicators.note: the letters are played with, moved around

explanation.surface: A reviewer panning the dreadful cast of a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: "Diabolical" sounds like a critic's verdict on the actors, but it is the literal devilish meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanic means of or like Satan, hence diabolical.

clue.text: Buccaneer finally turned libertine

indicators.note: take the last letter of turned

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute man

explanation.surface: A pirate who eventually became a debauchee.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Francis Drake was an Elizabethan privateer, which the Spanish counted as a pirate.
explanation.definitionFit: Drake raided Spanish ships and ports, a buccaneer in all but commission.

clue.text: A modification accepted by both sides in Russian port

indicators.note: the modification is taken in between the two sides

parts.note: right and left, R and L

explanation.surface: An amendment that both parties agree to in a Russian harbour negotiation.
explanation.walkthrough: "Both sides" sounds like two negotiating parties but gives R and L, right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: Archangel (Arkhangelsk) is a port on the White Sea in northern Russia.

clue.text: A new piece of advice regarding hors d'oeuvre

parts.note: a tip is a piece of advice

explanation.surface: A fresh suggestion about what to serve as a starter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as menu advice, which is exactly where the answer belongs.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is the Italian hors d'oeuvre served before the pasta.

clue.text: Soak up air circulating in strange animal enclosure

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to ret is to soak flax or hemp to soften it

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the word for strange

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange

indicators.note: circulating moves these letters around into a new order

explanation.surface: Damp air circulates inside a strange cage for animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum here is the old British adjective meaning odd, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrarium is a glass case for keeping small land animals or plants.

clue.text: Wide boy in poem always after tennis equipment

indicators.note: the poetic always comes after the tennis equipment

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A spiv in a poem forever chasing tennis kit.
explanation.walkthrough: A wide boy is British slang for a small-time crook or spiv.
explanation.definitionFit: A racketeer runs dishonest schemes, as a wide boy does.

clue.text: European king in ceremony connected to American state

indicators.note: connected to means the American letter is joined on at the end
in means the king letter goes inside the ceremony word

parts.note: R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A European monarch takes part in a ceremony linked to an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a US state, but the answer is a country in East Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Eritrea is a sovereign country on the Red Sea coast, so a state in the political sense.

clue.text: Silence about limits of unusual prison

indicators.note: take the outer letters of unusual

parts.note: first and last letters of UnusuaL

explanation.surface: Hushing up the extent of an unusual jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer: the gulag was where dissidents were silenced.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulag was the Soviet system of forced-labour prison camps.

clue.text: Sailing ship in strong wind about to cross lake

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

explanation.surface: A sailing ship in a gale, about to cross a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: "About to cross" reads as on the point of crossing; ON is about, and GALE takes in L.
explanation.definitionFit: A galleon is a large square-rigged sailing ship.

clue.text: Child in game extremely curious about boxer's slanting script

parts.note: in tag the child doing the chasing is 'it'

indicators.note: about here means on or around, so the end letters attach to the boxer, placed after him

parts.note: Muhammad Ali was the famous heavyweight boxer

indicators.note: extremely means the two end letters of curious

explanation.surface: A child in a game is very curious about a boxer's handwriting.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of boxer's is kept as a letter, and 'extremely' takes just one extreme of curious, which sits before that S.
explanation.definitionFit: Italics is a typeface whose letters slope to the right, so it is a sloping style of print.

clue.text: Direct course of ox, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a verb: guide the path of a vehicle or ship
a noun: a young castrated bull, 'perhaps' because an ox is only one example

explanation.surface: Guiding the path of an ox.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses sit naturally together, which hides the join between them: you might well steer a steer.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers a helmsman's verb and a cattle farmer's noun, the young bullock raised for beef.

clue.text: Key singers upset following lines using celebs only

indicators.note: following means the reversed singers come after the lines

parts.note: L is an abbreviation for line, so LL is lines

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: rats sing, informing to the police

explanation.surface: A choir in a key gets upset following the lines of a show with only stars.
explanation.walkthrough: Singers are informers, rats who sing to the police; upset turns RATS into STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-star cast is made up entirely of famous performers, so the event features only celebrities.

clue.text: Encountered going north, work up speed

indicators.note: going north in a down clue means the letters run from the bottom up
in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom

explanation.surface: Meeting someone heading north who urges you to work faster.
explanation.walkthrough: "Work up speed" looks like a phrase meaning accelerate, but it splits into wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is speed, especially the pace of music.

clue.text: African country reflecting about mother's ruin

indicators.note: as in a mirror, the letters read backwards

parts.note: mother's ruin is British slang for gin

explanation.surface: A country pondering the disgrace of someone's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother's ruin is an old British nickname for gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Niger is a landlocked country in West Africa.

clue.text: Like protective layer originally required to stop widespread disease

indicators.note: to stop means the letter plugs a gap inside the disease word

parts.note: an epidemic is a disease spreading widely

indicators.note: originally means only the first letter of required

explanation.surface: Protection was needed from the start to halt a spreading illness.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into EPIDEMIC after its D.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the outer layer of skin that shields the body, so epidermic describes that covering.

clue.text: Healthy food: price reduced by 25 per cent

indicators.note: reduced by 25 per cent keeps three of the four letters, cutting the last

explanation.surface: A health food whose price has dropped by a quarter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cos is a type of crisp lettuce, a salad green seen as wholesome.

clue.text: Pulse ideally occurring at periodic intervals

indicators.note: letters that occur at regular intervals are every second one, so take alternate letters

explanation.surface: A heartbeat that ideally comes at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: "Pulse" suggests a heartbeat, matching the regular-interval surface; it is the lentil kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Dal is split lentils or other pulses, and the dish made from them.

clue.text: Acerbic representation of Maori cousin

indicators.note: the letters are re-presented in a new order

explanation.surface: A sharp-tongued portrayal of a New Zealand relative.
explanation.walkthrough: A clean anagram; the surface is a family portrait with bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimonious means bitter and sharp, as acerbic does.
